abstracts.abstract: The increasing complexity of heterogeneous network architectures necessitates a fundamental rethinking of protocol design methodologies. This paper presents a novel information-theoretic framework for network protocol synthesis that fundamentally departs from conventional approach-based design paradigms. Unlike existing approaches that rely on heuristic optimization and empirical tuning, our framework establishes rigorous mathematical foundations by characterizing network communication as a compression-distortion trade-off problem. We formalize protocol behavior as a constrained Markov decision process, where protocol states correspond to information-theoretic quantities that can be systematically optimized. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that optimal protocols must satisfy a minimum description length principle, leading to inherent trade-offs between network efficiency and robustness. Furthermore, we prove that our framework naturally subsumes existing protocol design methodologies as special cases under specific parameter regimes. Simulation results across diverse network scenarios—including wireless mesh networks, mobile ad hoc networks, and software-defined networking environments—validate the theoretical predictions and demonstrate substantial performance improvements. The proposed paradigm shift enables protocol designers to systematically explore the protocol design space with theoretical guarantees, marking a departure from the traditional trial-and-error methodology that has dominated computer communications research for decades.

Accurate network performance evaluation under realistic traffic conditions remains a critical challenge in computer communications research. Traditional queueing-theoretic models often fail to capture the complex burstiness and long-range dependence characteristic of modern network traffic. This paper proposes an enhanced analytical framework based on_fractional Brownian motion (fBm) that significantly improves upon existing performance prediction models. Our approach introduces a novel traffic characterization method that jointly captures both short-range and long-range dependence through a generalized Hurst parameter estimation technique. We develop closed-form expressions for key performance metrics including queuing delay, packet loss probability, and throughput under non-stationary traffic conditions. The analytical framework is validated through extensive numerical simulations and trace-driven experiments using real network traffic data from operational network environments. Results demonstrate that our model reduces prediction error by up to 45% compared to conventional methods while maintaining analytical tractability. The proposed framework provides network designers with powerful tools for capacity planning and quality-of-service provisioning in data center networks and wireless networking scenarios where accurate performance prediction is essential for efficient resource allocation.

The emergence of edge computing paradigms demands a fundamental rearchitecting of how network functions are deployed and orchestrated. This paper presents EdgeAI-Net, a revolutionary network architecture that embeds machine learning capabilities directly into the network fabric, fundamentally transforming the paradigm of software-defined networking. Unlike conventional SDN architectures that separate control and data planes through static rule-based forwarding, EdgeAI-Net introduces a continuously self-optimizing network plane where distributed neural networks perform real-time traffic classification, resource allocation, and fault prediction. We design a hierarchical controller architecture that coordinates learning across edge nodes while maintaining global network stability through a novel consensus mechanism. The system incorporates programmable data planes with custom neural processing units that enable inference at line rate without introducing excessive latency overhead. Deployment experiments in a realistic edge computing testbed demonstrate that EdgeAI-Net achieves adaptive quality-of-service provisioning, intelligent load balancing, and proactive security mechanisms—all operating autonomously without manual intervention. This work establishes a new design philosophy for computer communications networks where artificial intelligence is not merely an application running on the network, but an intrinsic component of the network infrastructure itself.

Scalability limitations in centralized software-defined networking controllers create significant bottlenecks in large-scale network deployments. This paper introduces DistroFlow, an improved distributed control plane architecture that substantially enhances the scalability and responsiveness of SDN networks. Our design addresses the fundamental challenge of maintaining consistent network-wide state across geographically distributed controllers through a novel hierarchical synchronization mechanism that reduces control plane communication overhead by 60% compared to existing solutions. DistroFlow implements a two-tier architecture comprising regional controllers that handle local traffic patterns while maintaining eventual consistency with a global state repository. We propose adaptive load balancing algorithms that dynamically redistribute flow rule installations based on real-time traffic matrices, achieving significant improvements in controller utilization efficiency. Security mechanisms are incorporated to protect control plane communications through lightweight cryptographic protocols that add minimal latency overhead. Evaluation on a testbed emulating production-scale data center networks with up to 10,000 switches demonstrates that DistroFlow achieves 40% lower average flow setup latency and maintains 99.99% consistency guarantee under realistic failure scenarios. This work provides network operators with a practical solution for deploying SDN in enterprise and data center environments requiring high scalability.
